en: A cone-shaped cloth tube that shows wind direction and strength; used as a road-sign symbol.
Bright red lights at the back of a vehicle used only in thick fog to help others see you.
Water thrown up by tyres on a wet road, which can reduce visibility.
A curve in the road that turns to the right as you travel along it.
A raised ridge across the road that forces drivers to slow down.
Anti-lock braking system that helps you steer while braking hard in an emergency.
Braking as quickly and safely as possible to avoid a collision.
To roll without engine drive (e.g. in neutral), which reduces control.
Anti-lock braking system that helps you steer while braking hard in an emergency.
The main brake pedal operated with your foot to slow or stop the vehicle.
How well the tyres hold the road surface for steering and braking.
Moving off from a standstill on an uphill slope without rolling back.
How deep the grooves in a tyre are; worn-down tread reduces grip, especially in wet weather.
A caravan being pulled behind another vehicle on the road.
A device that helps reduce swaying of a trailer or caravan while towing.
The shafts that the wheels of a vehicle or trailer turn on.
A frame fitted on a vehicle’s roof for carrying extra loads.
Straps, ropes, or other fittings used to hold a load firmly in place.
A marked place on the road where people on foot can cross safely.
Driving with too little space behind another vehicle (tailgating), which is unsafe.
How long you have to react and brake before you would hit the vehicle ahead.
A rule of thumb: stay at least two seconds behind the vehicle ahead in good, dry conditions.
Moves out to the right before turning left—common for long vehicles that need more space.
White diamond road markings that show a lane reserved for particular vehicles.
Briefly switch headlights on and off only to let others know you are there—not to claim priority.
Who is allowed to go first when paths cross or meet.
An amber traffic light that blinks on and off at a pelican crossing.
A careful driving style that anticipates hazards and leaves a safety margin.
Moving livestock (such as sheep or cattle) along or across a road.
A flashing blue warning light used by certain emergency or specialist vehicles.
A vehicle that clears snow from the road, often with a blade at the front.
A vehicle that helps remove or repair broken-down vehicles on the road.
Headlights aimed high for maximum range; can dazzle oncoming drivers.
Pedestrian traffic lights started by pressing a button at the crossing.
In good, dry conditions, keep at least a two-second gap behind the vehicle ahead.
The cover that seals the diesel filler opening; if loose, fuel can spill onto the road.
The high-intensity headlight setting (full beam) for dark roads with no oncoming traffic.
A road with many bends, where overtaking is often difficult and slow traffic can build up.
Briefly switches headlights on and off—often to ask for room to pass, not to demand you speed up.
The cover that seals the fuel tank opening after refuelling.
A flashing green warning light used by certain medical vehicles responding to emergencies.
A vehicle that spreads salt or grit on roads to reduce ice in cold weather.
Pass a person riding a horse on the road; horses can be startled by noise and speed.
Electric passenger vehicles that run on rails set into the road surface.
A road with no street lighting at night.
Moves suddenly into your lane or gap with little space in front of you.
Emergency warning lights used by police, fire, ambulance, and similar services.
Blinding other drivers with bright lights, such as brake lights in a queue at night.
Left alone with no one in or watching the vehicle.
The outer shell and panels of the vehicle (bonnet, wings, doors, etc.).
The busiest times of day when roads are most congested (rush hour).
A liquid mixed with water in the cooling system to stop it freezing in cold weather.
Hydraulic fluid that transfers pressure from the brake pedal to the brakes.
Dim sidelights left on when parked so others can see your vehicle at night.
Not moving; the vehicle is at a complete stop.
The official paper (V5C / log book) that records who the vehicle is registered to.
A car radio that needs a code after power loss, making it useless to thieves.
Busy periods when many people travel, often morning and evening rush hours.
Heavy, slow-moving traffic when roads are overcrowded.
How much fuel the vehicle uses; higher use means more cost and emissions.
Tyres with too little air pressure, which can worsen handling and wear.
Painted lines on the road that show where each traffic lane is.
A system that warns if a vehicle is in an area you cannot see in your mirrors.
How fast the engine is turning; often shown on the rev counter (tachometer).
Gradually moving sideways so the vehicle leaves its traffic lane.
The vehicle steers or veers left or right by itself when you brake or drive.
Braking suddenly and hard instead of smoothly and early.
A parking or traffic warden who enforces parking rules.
Rubber or metal rings that stop oil leaking from the engine.
A belt that keeps engine valves and pistons moving in the correct timing.
The pedal/system that disconnects the engine from the wheels when changing gear.
The maker’s planned times for checks, oil changes, and maintenance.
A map or app that suggests roads and directions for a journey.
The vehicle’s owner manual with operating and safety information.
Causing less harm to the environment, e.g. lower emissions.
A different path to the same destination if the usual road is blocked.
Fees charged to drive into certain busy city zones to reduce traffic.
Lanes reserved mainly for buses (and sometimes taxis or cycles).
The part of the car that contains the gears for changing speed and power.
The system that transfers engine power to the wheels, including the gearbox.
